opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is that the project has to solve a real problem that a lot of people actually have. It sounds obvious, but many open-source projects start from "this is technically interesting" rather than "people are struggling with this every day." When I look at projects that really take off, there's usually a moment where the pain is very widespread. For LLM inference, for example, suddenly everyone wanted to serve these large models, and serving them efficiently was hard. If you show up with something that works at that moment, people come to you.

The second layer is that it has to be easy to get started. The first five minutes matter a lot. If someone can `pip install` it, run one command, and see it working, you've won a user. If they have to fight with dependencies for two days, most people just leave. A lot of the unglamorous work, like packaging, documentation, CI, and making sure it runs on different hardware, is what keeps people around, even though nobody writes papers about it.

The third layer, which I think is the hardest, is the community and governance side. Early on, a small group of people can carry a project on passion. That doesn't scale. As the project grows you get contributions from many companies, many hardware vendors, many researchers, and their interests don't always align. Someone wants to add their feature, someone else worries it makes the codebase messy. So you need maintainers who are willing to say no, to keep the architecture clean, and to make decisions transparently so contributors trust the process. A lot of my time actually goes into this: reviewing PRs, refactoring things so new contributors can plug in more easily, and trying to make the codebase something people can understand rather than a pile of patches.

And finally, sustainability means someone has to be paid to care. Pure volunteer effort burns out. The healthy pattern I've seen is that the project becomes important enough that many companies depend on it, and then they have an incentive to fund people to work on it, through sponsoring, hiring maintainers, or contributing engineers. It becomes a kind of shared infrastructure, where everyone benefits from it being good, so everyone chips in. If you can reach that point, where the project is neutral and many parties invest in it, it can sustain itself for a long time. If it's controlled by just one company, there's always a risk that their priorities change and the project fades.

So in short: a real problem, a low barrier to entry, good governance, and an ecosystem of stakeholders who have a reason to keep it alive.

r001.rationale: The response says a project must solve a real problem that many people have and describes widespread pain as what helps projects take off.

r002.rationale: It says companies can fund maintainers or contribute engineers, but does not state that a startup company must organize the project's operation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot because of my work on vLLM, and my honest answer is that growth and sustainability are two different problems, and people often confuse them.

Growth is actually the easier part. An open-source project grows when it solves a real pain point at the right moment. For vLLM, that moment was when everyone suddenly needed to serve large language models and realized that naive inference was wasting most of the GPU memory. PagedAttention addressed that directly, and the project took off almost on its own. Timing and a genuinely useful idea do most of the work there. You cannot manufacture that with marketing.

Sustaining the project is much harder, and I think it comes down to three things.

The first is a community that actually feels ownership. In the early days, most of the code comes from a small core team. But if it stays that way, the project dies when those people get tired or move on. You have to make it genuinely easy and rewarding for outsiders to contribute. That means reviewing pull requests quickly, explaining why something is rejected instead of just closing it, and giving people real responsibility once they have proven themselves. Many of our most active maintainers started as users who hit a bug, fixed it, and were treated well enough that they stayed.

The second is being the neutral ground. In the inference space, there are many hardware vendors, many model providers, and many companies with their own agendas. An open-source project becomes sustainable when all of those parties see it as a place they can invest without handing an advantage to a competitor. NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and the various model labs all contribute to vLLM partly because none of them owns it. That neutrality is a real asset, and you have to protect it deliberately. The moment a project is seen as one company's product in disguise, the broader community pulls back.

The third thing is a bit less romantic, which is engineering discipline. Popular projects get flooded with features, and every feature is a maintenance burden forever. You need people willing to say no, to keep the architecture clean, and to do unglamorous work like testing, performance regression tracking, and documentation. Nobody gets famous for fixing CI, but a project with broken CI loses contributors very fast.

If I had to add one more, it would be that the maintainers need a way to make a living. Passion carries you for a year or two. Beyond that, you need either companies employing people to work on the project full-time, or some kind of foundation or funding structure. Burnout is probably the most common reason good open-source projects quietly fade away, and it is almost never talked about until it is too late.

r001.rationale: It says a project grows by solving a real pain point at the right moment, illustrated by widespread need for LLM serving.

r002.rationale: It says sustainability needs maintainers to earn a living through company employment or a foundation or funding structure, but does not say a startup company must organize the project’s operation.

astra-6.text:
I think an open-source project needs to solve a real problem first. People need a reason to use it, and that value has to be clear enough that they’re willing to spend time trying it.

But to sustain it, you need more than useful code. You need good documentation, maintainers who respond to questions, and a welcoming path for people to contribute. Someone might start by reporting a bug or fixing a small issue. If that experience is positive, they may become a regular contributor.

And you have to make the maintenance sustainable. If everything depends on one person’s free time, that’s fragile. So I’d focus on building a community that can share responsibility, with clear priorities and realistic expectations.

r001.rationale: It says the project should solve a real problem and offer clear value, but does not say widespread interest in that problem is a prerequisite for growing large.

r002.rationale: It discusses sustainable maintenance and shared community responsibility, but does not state that a startup company must organize the project's operation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an open-source project needs to solve a real problem first. People come because it helps them do something, and they stay because it works reliably and keeps improving.

But sustaining it takes more than good code. You need to make it easy for people to participate—clear documentation, responsive discussions, and a path from reporting an issue to making a contribution. If everything depends on one maintainer, growth can actually become a burden.

So I would focus on building a community where people can gradually take ownership. And maintainers need support, whether that’s funding, time from their employers, or other contributors sharing the work. The project has to be sustainable for the people behind it, too.

r001.rationale: The response says the project should solve a real problem and attract users, but does not say that widespread interest in that problem is needed for the project to grow large.

r002.rationale: The response discusses maintainers, community participation, and support, but does not state that a startup company must organize the project’s operation.
